_note: One creator's public tier lists, shown on a part's detail sheet under a credit link. Not BeyClub's writing and not one of the three ranking sources — display only, they never reach blendRating(). `sources` is keyed by the catalogue's part category, so each category carries its own video, its own credit and its own tier names: the bit video grades Top Level / Meta Relevant / Niche Picks / Not Worth Using / What Are You Doing, the ratchet video Top Level / Situational Choices / Niche Picks / Do You Want To Lose? / Plastic Waste. Those are the creator's labels, not our grade scale, so do not normalise them into one set — a colour for each lives in PICK_TIER_COLORS in PartSheet.tsx. `parts` holds the catalogue codes an entry covers; it is a list because a video may rate several parts together, as the bit one does with the six gear bits. `at` is the point in that source's video, in seconds, and becomes a ?t= deep link. `note` is one trimmed sentence, at most 140 characters — the detail sheet is already long and this section is meant to stay three lines. The sheet lists NR/Nr and OP/Op as two rows each — one physical bit listed twice, not two parts — and the duplicate lowercase row is dropped in partOverrides.json, so forCode() case-folds to reach a pick keyed on either casing.

credit.author: ToxicShark
credit.sourceName: Ranking EVERY Bit In Beyblade X

picks.note: Single-handedly elevates left-spin blades through spin equalization, and finishes well on spin.
Top-tier stamina — keeps more spin on the rails than Ball, and is safer to hard-launch in Rod mirrors.
The best stamina bit among the high burst-resistance options; it tanks hits and stabilizes well.
The longest spin time of any aggressive balance bit, and a versatile anti-attack pick under top-heavy CX combos.
Arguably the best bit in the game once mastered — exceptional endgame stamina and KO power, high skill ceiling.
Extremely consistent and highly controlled attack, with low gears and solid endgame stamina.
The former number one and still a top stamina pick, though Free Ball is safer on the rails.
Aggressive with enough LAD to outspin attack types, but it bleeds stamina on the rail if misplayed.
Stationary stamina and defense — a lower centre of gravity and smaller contact patch grip the stadium well.
A more aggressive Rush, but the launch tech is harder and the result more volatile.
A smaller face than Flat preserves more energy on the rails, but the top attack bits outclass it.
Low rail stamina loss and high ratchet burst resistance, though it spun shorter than Free Ball in testing.
The classic balance bit that once won tournaments, now outclassed by Kick, Level and Jolt.
Terrible brand new, but a strong counter-attacker with good grip and stamina once worn down.
Solid endgame stamina for a balance-attack bit, but the newer balance bits have passed it.
The lowest attack bit there is — useful for specific ratchet-sniper builds.
A stationary landmine bit that moves smoothly; good against inexperienced players, limited against pros.
A low gear count gives controlled rail movement, but it leans over and destabilizes.
A wider Point — it can outspin Cobalt Dragoon on Elevate with the right blade, but Point and Level are better.
Inconsistent and topples over easily; its wins are anomalies you cannot repeat.
A budget Rush replacement, but too fast with too many gears to control.
The extra bottom friction never turns into real defense and drains stamina quickly.
The early-game attack standard, now completely outclassed on stamina by modern attack bits.
Used briefly on Cobalt Dragoon for minor LAD before Elevate arrived, but its stamina is weak.
Noticeably worse than a standard Taper because of the raised centre of gravity.
A niche ratchet-sniper bit from an earlier meta with no competitive stamina left.
Gimmicky, prone to bursting, and outclassed on every metric.
Not bad in itself, just redundant next to Free Ball, Ball and Low Orb.
A height-adjustable Kick — raising the centre of gravity only makes it worse than standard Kick.
Its theoretical balance utility never shows up in results; Point and Kick outclass it.
A budget Rush alternative that lacks control and is heavily outclassed by Rush and Low Rush.
The wall ring adds no defense while adding burst risk and rail stamina drain.
Excessive gears kill stamina on the rail — strictly worse than Flat.
Drastically raises height and burst risk; the recent tournament wins are anomalies.
Extremely high burst risk and poor performance.
Hyper-volatile and prone to self-extremes — only worth it as a high-variance panic option for beginners.
The high centre of gravity destabilizes the bey and leaves the ratchet easy to snipe.
Uncontrollable movement and abysmal stamina.
Gimmicky and ineffective across almost every competitive build.
Banned from official tournament play because it damages stadium surfaces.
Stationary centre-docking with low burst resistance — an easy target for attack types.
The worst bit in the game; the jumping gimmick ruins both balance and stamina.
Stationary, with low burst resistance and poor stamina.
Inferior face geometry and needless height options make it worse than standard Point.
Horrible burst resistance, and the gimmick fires late when there is no energy left to KO with.
Low stability, high burst risk and terrible stamina.
Unbelievably loose in the ratchet — extremely burst-prone and unusable.

credit.author: ToxicShark
credit.sourceName: Ranking EVERY Ratchet In Beyblade X

picks.note: One of the best ratchets in the game — pocket-jumping and one-sided weight bias at the optimal height, and good on anything.
A heavy, well-balanced jack of all trades that is rarely the wrong call on attack or stamina; almost always worth a deck slot.
The best ratchet in Beyblade X — the least burst-prone in the game, well balanced, and the pick if you could run only one.
All the one-sided perks, but the 50-height clip rattles, so keep it to aggressive builds on high burst-resistance bits.
A good ratchet, used mainly to match a 1-60's height on a second blade; little reason to pick it over the 1-60 itself.
Untested at the time of the video — the low height should offset the five-sided burst risk, but its place in the meta is unclear.
Heavy, balanced and good on stamina but more burst-prone than its rivals; Phoenix on 5-60 Point once led the balance meta.
Seven-sided is the heaviest family, so it limits self-recoil on smash builds, and its thicker side can offset an imbalanced blade.
A tight one is still usable — the nine-sided round profile resists bursting enough to carry the extra height.
Tall builds are usually a mistake, but Aero Pegasus on Rush with it won a lot more than it lost at a high level.
Hard to find a reason for, beyond raising a Low Rush build slightly when you don't want to spend the 1-70.
Was a fine low-profile pick before the 1-50 existed, and still is if you lack one, but it rattles and four-sided bursts.
Well balanced but loose and unusually light, so it adds neither weight nor burst resistance; heavier options do more.
The only simple ratchet worth a look — by far Clock Mirage's best, and it bursts far less than the 4-55 does.
One of the better 70-heights — it saw Tyranno Beat play once, and it still beats everything below it.
Heavy, but 70-height and largely untested — it sits at the very bottom of the tier on secondhand reports.
A last resort — the same idea as the 9-70 but worse, saved only by being a nine-sided ratchet.
Bottom-mounted protrusions catch the rail, so it self-bursts and kills its own stamina; the low height makes it the worst of the two.
Still not good, but the extra height keeps the protrusions off the rail, so it edges out the 0-60.
A simple ratchet, so incredibly burst-prone; only the low 55-height keeps it out of plastic waste on Clock Mirage.
Four-sided protrusions stick out awkwardly and get hit, so it stays burst-prone even at the best height.
Simply a worse 6-60, though not as bad as the plastic waste below it.
80-height raises the centre of gravity, so it destabilises easily and is a sitting duck for any attack type to snipe.
The best of the two-sided heights, which only means the least awful — the huge protrusions are burst on far too easily.
Two-sided protrusions are enormous and burst on contact, and the extra height only makes it worse than the 2-60.
Possibly the second worst ratchet in the game — two-sided burst risk stacked on an 80-height's instability.
The 3-60's late-game lean becomes a collapse at 80-height; it destabilises and bursts far too easily.
The worst ratchet in the game — a simple ratchet's lock means no bit can make it burst-resistant, at maximum height.
Four-sided burst risk at 70-height — roughly on par with the 3-80, and nowhere near usable.
Worse than the 4-70, and arguably worse than the 2-60 — burst-prone and top-heavy at the same time.
If the 5-60 is already burst-prone, the 5-70 is worse, and the extra height buys nothing back.
A bad ratchet — five-sided burst risk at the worst possible height.
An 80-height six-sided ratchet: loose, light and burst-prone all at once.
Heavy, but far too tall, so things simply tip over — and it is incredibly burst-prone because of it.
Goes the way of the other 80-heights — too tall to be anything but a liability.
A simple ratchet, and worse than the 55-height ones, so it bursts very easily — the best of a bad tier.
As heavy as it looks, but it bursts if you breathe on it — among the very worst ratchets in the game.
